rationale: B wins because it is more disciplined about turning missing proof into gates instead of dressing gaps as facts. Its strongest line, "Warby Parker says store shoppers spend more than online buyers. It will not say how much," is a real reporter question with a built-in kill switch. A has strong shapes, but "Warby Parker's retail expansion means a large new employer of optometrists" declares an employment model the update explicitly has not proven.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker was supposed to make optical stores obsolete" overstates the founding contradiction from facts not supplied in the update.
"Warby Parker's retail expansion means a large new employer of optometrists" assumes Warby is the employer before the employment or contracting model is known.

"healthcare access reporter tracking where Americans can get optical care without visiting a specialty store" stretches the pharmacy pilot; the update says glasses through a pharmacy chain, not exams or care delivery there.
"choosing where to deploy earnings" is investor-sounding filler unless filings show the expansion is funded from profits rather than ordinary capital allocation.
gaps_in_B: "the company that made direct-to-consumer eyewear a category" imports brand-history context not present in the supplied update.
"it is the reason the whole expansion exists" turns Warby's retail-spend claim into causation without proof.
"drugstore shelves" may imply a shelf retail execution the update does not specify; the pilot could be a different pharmacy-channel model.

It may over-refuse the workforce angle: "Warby Parker is hiring optometrists at scale as the profession shifts to retail" is not just a duplicate if the protagonist is independent optometry practices and the employment model can be proven.
